lesson.title: Biotechnology in modern medicine
lesson.scope: Connect recombinant proteins, gene therapy and cell replacement with their distinct purposes.

screens.title: Recap: Modern Integration
screens.html:
RECAP

Recap: Modern Integration

Modern medicine now relies on Recombinant DNA to produce human proteins. This has replaced the extraction of hormones from animal sources, which often caused allergic reactions or carried risks of infection.

screens.title: The Role of Regulation
screens.html:
The Role of Regulation

Safeguarding the Public

In Australia, the Therapeutic Goods Administration (TGA) regulates all medical treatments. This ensures that biotechnology tools like mRNA vaccines are safe, effective, and ethically produced.

screens.title: SYLLABUS REVIEW
screens.html:
SYLLABUS REVIEW

Syllabus Focus: ATAR Standards

WA Year 12 Human Biology covers treating Endocrine and Nervous system dysfunctions.

Endocrine System - Synthetic hormones and Gene Therapy for Diabetes.

Nervous System - Cell Therapy for Alzheimer’s and Parkinson’s.

screens.title: Synthetic Hormones Review
screens.html:
🧠

Synthetic Hormones Review

Diabetes and Thyroid Control

We use recombinant DNA to create Insulin (for Diabetes Mellitus) and Thyroxine (for Hypothyroidism). This involves inserting the human gene into a bacterial host like E. coli.

Remember

Hormones produced this way are chemically identical to human naturally occurring hormones.

screens.title: Gene Therapy for Diabetes
screens.html:
🔑

Gene Therapy for Diabetes

Method

Using a viral vector to deliver a functional insulin-producing gene into the patient's cells.

Outcome

The goal is to allow the patient’s own body to regulate blood glucose without external injections.

Key point

Gene therapy targets the root genetic cause, whereas synthetic hormones only treat the symptoms.

screens.html:

screens.title: Hormone vs. Gene Therapy
screens.html:
Hormone vs. Gene Therapy

Gene therapy is currently the primary clinical treatment for most Type 1 diabetics in Australia.

👎​

Why is that?

a) Gene therapy is still largely in clinical trial phases, whereas synthetic hormone therapy is the established standard care.

b) Synthetic hormones are more expensive than gene therapy, so they are preferred by hospitals.

screens.title: REVIEW
screens.html:
REVIEW

CRT: Nervous System Disorders

Cell Replacement Therapy (CRT) treats conditions where neurons are lost.

Parkinson's: Replacing dopamine-producing cells in the substantia nigra.

Alzheimer's: Replacing cholinergic neurons to restore memory pathways.

screens.title: The Quality of Life Impact
screens.html:
The Quality of Life Impact

How do we measure the success of biotechnology? For a patient with Parkinson's, success might be regaining the ability to walk or write. For an ATAR exam, you must argue the social and economic benefits of these treatments.

screens.title: Biotechnology Career Paths
screens.html:
Biotechnology Career Paths

Biomedical Scientist

Designing and testing new recombinant DNA tools in research labs.

Regulatory Affairs

Working for the TGA or clinical trials to ensure new treatments are safe.

Genetic Counsellor

Helping families understand their genetic risks and therapy options.

screens.title: Bioinformatics: The Future
screens.html:
🤯

Bioinformatics: The Future

Processing Big Data

Bioinformatics uses computer algorithms to map the human genome and predict how people will react to certain drugs. This forms the basis of Personalised Medicine.

Fun fact

The first human genome sequence took 13 years; now it can be done in under 24 hours.

screens.title: Ethical Considerations
screens.html:
Ethical Considerations

The use of embryonic stem cells in CRT and the potential for 'designer babies' through gene editing remain hot topics in Australian ethics committees.

screens.title: Exam Prep: Structure
screens.html:
Exam Prep: Structure

Answering Extended Responses

When asked about 'Implications', always structure your answer into three categories:

Personal (health outcome)

Economic (cost to government)

Social (ethical acceptance)

screens.title: KEY CONCEPT
screens.html:
KEY CONCEPT

Case Study: Parkinson's CRT

The success of CRT for Parkinson's depends on the successful integration of transplanted cells into the existing brain circuitry.

screens.title: The Future of Vaccines
screens.html:
The Future of Vaccines

Beyond COVID-19

Recombinant DNA technology is being used to develop vaccines for Malaria and HIV. These rely on the production of viral antigens without using the actual pathogen.

screens.title: DISCUSSION
screens.html:
DISCUSSION

Global Health Inequity

The Gap

Rich nations have access to the latest therapies. Poor nations often lack the basic cold-chain infrastructure to store them.

Health is a human right, but biotechnology is currently a privilege. — Anonymous Bioethicist

screens.title: Examining WA Standards
screens.html:
⚠️

Examining WA Standards

In WA, the Human Biology exam expects you to demonstrate how biotechnology satisfies Science as a Human Endeavour. This means showing the interaction between science and society.

Watch out

Don't just list the steps of PCR; explain WHY we need it for medical diagnosis.

screens.title: Synthesis of Learning
screens.html:
Synthesis of Learning

Biotechnology is the ultimate multidisciplinary field. It combines genetics, cell biology, computer science, and ethics to solve the most pressing problems of the human condition.

screens.title: Final Synthesis Task
screens.html:
Final Synthesis Task

If you were on an Australian ethics board, would you prioritise funding for synthetic hormone production (treating many) or gene therapy (curing a few)? Justify your answer using social and economic arguments.

screens.title: Final Synthesis Task
screens.html:
Final Synthesis Task

You might have said...

Prioritising synthetic hormones: Reaches more people, lower cost, proven safety, immediate quality of life impact.

Prioritising gene therapy: Long-term savings via one-time cure, prevents future costs, drives innovation, targets root causes.

questions.title: Written practice
questions.prompt: Compare recombinant protein therapy with gene augmentation for an inherited deficiency.
steps: Recombinant protein therapy supplies the required protein made outside the patient’s body.
Gene augmentation delivers a functional gene copy into target cells so they can produce a gene product.
Compare duration, delivery, effectiveness and risks using evidence rather than assuming either approach is a permanent cure.

bank.q: Which treatment supplies a missing protein without changing a patient’s DNA?
o: Inserting a therapeutic gene into patient cells
bank.why: A supplied recombinant protein can replace a deficient product without changing the patient’s genome.

bank.q: What is the main aim of gene augmentation?
o: Convert every cell into a stem cell
bank.why: Gene augmentation supplies a functional copy to support production of the required gene product.

bank.q: Why compare benefits with risks for biotechnology?
o: An intervention can have benefits and adverse effects
A mechanism alone proves clinical effectiveness
bank.why: Safety and effectiveness require evidence; a plausible mechanism alone is insufficient.
